COMPLETE TEXT & PAPER ROUTE

Make the numbers comparable.

Chapter 2: returns, compounding, present value and inflation. Suggested total 180 minutes, including setup, practice, checking and revision. No time limit; learner timings remain unvalidated.

1. Workspace · 10 minutes

Use paper or a local document and a calculator. No programming, financial account or dataset is required. Keep a dated record of each first attempt, correction and reason. In this paper route, use the check explanations after trying; progress does not automatically synchronise to the interactive app.

5% = 0.05, so 5% growth multiplies a balance by 1.05. The power 1.05² means multiplying by 1.05 twice. Dividing reverses multiplication. A power of 1/2 means a square root. Try £200 at 3%: £206.

Completion: attempt and correct every practice calculation; write a brief method/limitation reflection per lesson; run a controlled two-case inflation comparison and a hand check; reach 7/8 on independent questions with questions 3, 7 and 8 correct; respond to feedback and produce a calculation card. This is formative self-study without a credential.

02 · 25 MINUTES · Count the whole return.

A price change is only part of the story when an investment pays you cash.

Objective: Calculate a one-period total return and identify what it includes.

ONE PERIOD · NO EXTERNAL DEPOSITS OR WITHDRAWALS

Separate a pound gain from a return.

Suppose you buy one hypothetical share at £50. At the end of the year it is worth £52, and you have received a £1 cash distribution. Your price gain is £2. Your total gain is £3. Divide by the £50 starting price to make the gain comparable with an investment of a different size.

Total return = (ending price − starting price + cash distribution) ÷ starting priceMultiply the decimal by 100 for a percentage. Here: (52 − 50 + 1) ÷ 50 = 0.06 = 6%.

The price-only return is 4%, while the total return is 6%. A distribution is cash paid to the holder, such as a dividend. Include that receipt once. Do not add it again if an already supplied total-return series includes it.

This one-period formula treats the distribution as cash held to the period end, earning no extra return. Reinvestment within the year would need payment dates and reinvestment prices. Fees and taxes are zero in this example. New money added by an investor is an external cash flow, not investment performance; this simple formula does not handle those flows.

Predict before checking

A price falls by £4 but the investment pays £2. Does receiving cash necessarily make the total return positive? Explain to yourself, then use the new case below.

Practice and transfer

After the first calculation, attempt the second case before inspecting its feedback. Keep the negative sign when the net gain is a loss.

Write your answers before opening feedback. Use numbers without units while calculating, then label your final result. Currency and requested percentages round to 2 decimals.

  1. Buy at £100, end at £104, receive a £3 distribution. Total return (%)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Include both the price change and the distribution, then divide by the £100 starting value.

    (104 − 100 + 3) ÷ 100 × 100 = 7%. The price-only return is 4%.

  2. New case: buy at £80, end at £76, receive £2. Total return (%)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    The £2 receipt partly offsets a £4 capital loss. Keep the negative sign.

    (76 − 80 + 2) ÷ 80 × 100 = −2.5%. A distribution does not guarantee a positive total return.

Explain and revise

Explain why price return can differ from total return. State one cash-flow or cost assumption you would record.

Self-review: My method includes a distribution once, divides by the starting value, and states what the example omits.

Write at least one specific correction or check and its reason. Confidence is optional and ungraded.

03 · 25 MINUTES · Growth has a changing base.

Successive returns multiply. Their arithmetic average need not describe the growth of your money.

Objective: Calculate compound growth, a cumulative return and an annualised growth rate.

Worked example: interest can earn interest.

Begin with £1,000. Earn 10% over each of two years, keeping all gains invested. The first year earns £100, giving £1,100. The second earns 10% of £1,100, which is £110. The ending value is £1,210.

Future value = starting amount × (1 + annual rate)yearsUse rates as decimals: £1,000 × 1.10² = £1,210. The rate here is an annual effective rate: the full growth over one year.

With simple interest, interest is calculated only on the original principal: £1,000 × (1 + 0.10 × 2) = £1,200. That comparison assumes interest is not reinvested and earns no interest itself.

Changing returns

When yearly returns differ, multiply their growth factors. A +50% year followed by a −50% year leaves £100 × 1.50 × 0.50 = £75. The arithmetic mean return is 0%, but the cumulative return is −25%.

Cumulative return = (1 + r₁) × (1 + r₂) × … − 1All r values are decimals. Multiply the final result by 100 for a percentage.

Describe a multi-year result on an annual basis.

The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is the constant annual rate that would connect a starting value to an ending value. For exactly three years, £1,000 growing to £1,728 has CAGR (1,728 ÷ 1,000)1/3 − 1 = 20%.

CAGR = (ending value ÷ starting value)1 / years − 1Assume no external deposits or withdrawals. A calculator's power key may be labelled ^ or xʸ. A square root is the power 1/2.

Annualising describes a result; it does not forecast the next year or describe volatility. In this chapter periods are whole, equally spaced years. Monthly rates and quoted nominal annual rates need a different frequency conversion; do not silently treat them as annual effective rates.

Predict

Would a +20% year exactly cancel a −20% year? Think about the amount on which the second percentage acts before calculating below.

Practice and transfer

Use the first task to practise the multiplier, the second to diagnose an error, and the third to infer an equal annual rate.

Write your answers before opening feedback. Use numbers without units while calculating, then label your final result. Currency and requested percentages round to 2 decimals.

  1. £500 earns 8% at each year end, reinvested, for two years. Ending value (£)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Multiply £500 by 1.08 twice. Do not add 16% to the starting value.

    500 × 1.08² = £583.20. The simple-interest comparison would be £580.

  2. A return of +20% followed by −20%: cumulative return (%)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Start with £100. Multiply by 1.20, then by 0.80.

    100 × 1.20 × 0.80 = 96, so the cumulative return is −4%, despite the arithmetic average being 0%.

  3. £100 grows to £121 over exactly two years, with no external cash flows. CAGR (%)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Find the equal annual multiplier: (121 ÷ 100) raised to the power 1/2.

    (121 ÷ 100)^(1/2) − 1 = 0.10 = 10% per year. CAGR summarises a path; it does not describe its volatility.

Explain and revise

Describe the error in adding successive yearly returns. Explain one thing CAGR does not tell you.

Self-review: I multiplied growth factors, distinguished CAGR from an arithmetic mean, and did not call an annualised result a forecast.

Write at least one specific correction or check and its reason. Confidence is optional and ungraded.

04 · 30 MINUTES · Put cash flows on the same date.

Compounding moves money forward. Discounting expresses future money on a present-date basis.

Objective: Calculate a lump-sum present value and sum separately discounted bond cash flows.

Worked example: reverse the growth calculation.

A hypothetical payment of £1,210 is due exactly two years from today. At a chosen 10% annual effective discount rate, the equivalent amount today is £1,210 ÷ 1.10² = £1,000. We have reversed the earlier compounding calculation.

Present value = future payment ÷ (1 + discount rate)years until paymentThe result is in time-0 pounds. The discount rate is supplied for this teaching comparison, not a recommended investment rate.

A future pound is not automatically worth less in every possible rate environment. Here we use nonnegative rates. The choice of discount rate reflects the comparison and the cash flow's characteristics; a formula alone does not make an uncertain payment guaranteed.

A bond is a schedule, not one undated number.

Consider a hypothetical two-year bond: it pays £50 at the end of year 1, then £1,050 at the end of year 2. The final payment includes the last £50 coupon and £1,000 principal repayment. With a supplied 5% rate:

Worked bond: cash-flow timing and present values
DatePaymentCalculationTime-0 value
End of year 1£5050 ÷ 1.05£47.62
End of year 2£1,0501,050 ÷ 1.05²£952.38
Total£1,100 across two datesAdd discounted payments£1,000.00

Keep full precision while calculating and round the final sum to pennies. Adding £50 and £1,050 first and discounting the whole £1,100 for two years gives the first coupon the wrong date. Adding another £1,000 principal would count it twice.

Assumptions: annual payments, one constant annual effective discount rate, promised payments made in full, no fees or taxes. Actual bond pricing may require default and liquidity analysis, accrued interest, other payment frequencies and a rate for each maturity.

Predict

If the discount rate rises while the promised payments stay fixed, should their present value rise or fall? The denominator gets larger, so present value falls for these positive future cash flows. A useful comparison is £1,000 now versus £1,100 in two years: at 5%, the latter is worth about £997.73 today, slightly less than £1,000.

Practice and transfer

The new bond has a different coupon from the worked example. Write both discounted terms before entering their sum.

Write your answers before opening feedback. Use numbers without units while calculating, then label your final result. Currency and requested percentages round to 2 decimals.

  1. Receive £926.10 at the end of year 3. At a 5% annual effective discount rate, present value (£)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Divide by 1.05 three times, rather than subtracting 15%.

    926.10 ÷ 1.05³ = £800. All values are on the time-0 basis.

  2. A bond pays £20 at year 1 and £1,020 at year 2 (including principal). At 5%, total present value (£)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Discount the year-1 and year-2 payments separately, then add them.

    20 ÷ 1.05 + 1,020 ÷ 1.05² = £944.22. The last payment already includes the principal; do not add £1,000 again.

Explain and revise

Explain why the two bond payments need different exponents, and identify where principal is included.

Self-review: I used the payment dates, discounted each cash flow separately, counted principal once and stated that the rate was an assumption.

Write at least one specific correction or check and its reason. Confidence is optional and ungraded.

05 · 25 MINUTES · More pounds. More buying power?

Nominal value counts money. Real value adjusts for changes in the price level.

Objective: Calculate an exact real return and express a future balance in starting-year purchasing power.

Worked example: a growing balance can buy less.

You start with £1,000 and earn a 5% nominal return. The balance becomes £1,050. If prices rise 8% over the same year, the basket that cost £1,000 now costs £1,080. Your ending balance buys a smaller fraction of the basket.

Real return = (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1Use decimals. (1.05 ÷ 1.08 − 1) × 100 = −2.7778%, or −2.78% rounded.

Subtracting inflation, 5% − 8% = −3%, is a useful approximation for small rates, but it is not the exact calculation. It may be misleading when rates are larger or precision matters.

Starting-year purchasing power = nominal ending balance ÷ price-level growth factorFor one year here: £1,050 ÷ 1.08 = £972.22 in starting-year pounds.

For n years of constant annual inflation π, the price-level factor is (1 + π)n. Deflate the nominal ending balance by that factor. This is not the same operation as discounting a future contractual payment using an investment discount rate: state which question and rate you are using.

Make the units explicit.

A chart showing £1,600 in year 10 may mean nominal pounds, starting-year purchasing power, or a discounted present value. These are different quantities. Always label the date basis and the rate convention. A broad inflation index is also an approximation to an individual's spending experience.

The lab uses assumed annual effective rates, constant inflation, reinvested growth and no additional deposits. None of its rates is current market data. It has no forecast uncertainty or investment volatility, and it does not model taxes or fees.

Predict

Keep the nominal growth rate fixed and raise only inflation. What happens to the nominal ending balance? What happens to purchasing power? Write your expectation before opening the lab.

Practice and transfer

Use the second task to report a pound amount rather than a percentage. Keep the units distinct.

Write your answers before opening feedback. Use numbers without units while calculating, then label your final result. Currency and requested percentages round to 2 decimals.

  1. Nominal return 6%, inflation 4%, over the same year. Exact real return (%)? Round to 2 decimals.
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Use (1.06 ÷ 1.04 − 1) × 100. Subtraction is only an approximation.

    The exact real return is 1.9231%, or 1.92%. The 2% subtraction approximation differs.

  2. £1,000 grows by 3% while prices rise 5%. Ending purchasing power in starting-year pounds (£)?
    Hint, then feedback after trying

    Divide the £1,030 nominal ending value by the price-level multiplier 1.05.

    £1,030 ÷ 1.05 = £980.95 in starting-year pounds. Nominal growth can coexist with a loss of purchasing power.

Explain and revise

Explain why a positive nominal return can have a negative real return. Distinguish an inflation adjustment from discounting at an investment rate.

Self-review: I used the ratio formula for real return, labelled the value in starting-year pounds, and stated that the rates are hypothetical.

Write at least one specific correction or check and its reason. Confidence is optional and ungraded.

6. Paper growth lab · 35 minutes

Assumptions: £1,000 invested at time 0, 5% annual effective growth, annual reinvestment, 10 whole years, no external deposits, fees, taxes, default or volatility. A separate £2,000 payment is due at year 10; its present value uses the 5% opportunity rate. First predict what would change if only inflation rose.

  1. Scenario A: inflation is 3%. Calculate nominal ending balance = 1,000 × 1.05¹⁰; simple-interest comparison = 1,000 × (1 + 0.05 × 10); purchasing power = nominal balance ÷ 1.03¹⁰; real annual return = (1.05 ÷ 1.03 − 1) × 100; separate payment PV = 2,000 ÷ 1.05¹⁰.
  2. Scenario B: change only inflation to 6%. Repeat all calculations. Record both scenarios, even if one seems unattractive.
  3. Read the supplied annual tables below. Calculate the endpoints and check one intermediate year independently; you do not need to transcribe or recompute every row.
  4. Check the final nominal amount independently by growing the previous year's balance by 5%.
  5. Compare nominal growth, purchasing power and the separate payment's present value. Write a correction to your prediction or explain a check, and state a model limitation.

Lab feedback after both attempts

Both nominal ending balances are £1,628.89; both simple-interest balances are £1,500. The separate £2,000 payment has PV £1,227.83 in both scenarios. At 3% inflation, purchasing power is £1,212.05 and the real annual rate is 1.94%. At 6% inflation, purchasing power is approximately £909.57 and the real annual rate is −0.94%. Inflation changes buying power without changing the fixed nominal calculation. The PV uses the unchanged 5% discount rate, not inflation. Rates and payments are invented teaching inputs, not forecasts.

7. Independent check · 20 minutes

Use annual effective rates, year-end payments and no external deposits, fees or taxes. You need 7/8 correct including questions 3, 7 and 8. A calculator is allowed. Round all pound values and requested percentage results to two decimals. Attempt the entire case before reading the answer section. Correct your method and record why it changed. If first-time correct, explain a tempting wrong method you rejected. Case B provides an alternate fixed case.

Case A

  1. Buy at £200, end at £210 and receive £6. Total return (%)?
  2. £5,000 compounds at 6% annually for two years. Ending value (£)?
  3. A +25% year followed by a −20% year: cumulative return (%)?
  4. £1,000 becomes £1,331 in exactly three years, no external flows. CAGR (%)?
  5. £1,200 due at year 2, discounted at 5% annually. Present value (£)?
  6. Bond: £40 at year 1 and £1,040 at year 2. Discount at 5%. Present value (£)?
  7. Nominal return 4%, inflation 7%, over one year. Exact real return (%) to 2 decimals?
  8. Your lab grows a balance at a constant 5% for 10 years. Which statement is justified?
    1. The chosen rate guarantees future investment results
    2. The result is conditional on the stated rate, timing, reinvestment and cost assumptions
    3. A positive ending balance proves that risk has disappeared
Case A feedback: open after trying
  1. (210 − 200 + 6) ÷ 200 × 100 = 8%.
  2. 5,000 × 1.06² = £5,618.00.
  3. 1.25 × 0.80 − 1 = 0%.
  4. (1,331 ÷ 1,000)^(1/3) − 1 = 10%.
  5. 1,200 ÷ 1.05² = £1,088.44.
  6. 40 ÷ 1.05 + 1,040 ÷ 1.05² = £981.41.
  7. 1.04 ÷ 1.07 − 1 = −2.80% rounded.
  8. An assumed rate is an input, not a forecast. These calculations omit default, volatility and other real-market features.

Case B

  1. Buy at £1,000, end at £1,020 and receive £30. Total return (%)?
  2. £800 compounds at 4% annually for three years. Ending value (£)?
  3. A +10% year followed by a −10% year: cumulative return (%)?
  4. £2,000 becomes £2,420 in exactly two years, no external flows. CAGR (%)?
  5. £1,500 due at year 3, discounted at 4% annually. Present value (£)?
  6. Bond: £30 at year 1 and £1,030 at year 2. Discount at 4%. Present value (£)?
  7. Nominal return 3%, inflation 6%, over one year. Exact real return (%) to 2 decimals?
  8. A toy model uses a constant 4% rate for 20 years. Which conclusion is justified?
    1. The chosen rate guarantees future investment results
    2. The result is conditional on the stated rate, timing, reinvestment and cost assumptions
    3. A positive ending balance proves that risk has disappeared
Case B feedback: open after trying
  1. (1,020 − 1,000 + 30) ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 5%.
  2. 800 × 1.04³ = £899.89.
  3. 1.10 × 0.90 − 1 = −1%.
  4. (2,420 ÷ 2,000)^(1/2) − 1 = 10%.
  5. 1,500 ÷ 1.04³ = £1,333.49.
  6. 30 ÷ 1.04 + 1,030 ÷ 1.04² = £981.14.
  7. 1.03 ÷ 1.06 − 1 = −2.83% rounded.
  8. An assumed rate is an input, not a forecast. These calculations omit default, volatility and other real-market features.

8. Calculation card · 10 minutes

Use a lab run or the bond example. Write: (1) inputs, payment dates, rate convention, formula and result; (2) the hand check and controlled comparison; (3) a limitation and a specific correction or check after feedback. Self-review the unit (percentage or pounds), date basis, nominal/real distinction and assumptions. Prose quality is self-reviewed, not machine validated.

Exemplar after drafting

“With £1,000 at time 0, 5% annual effective growth and 3% inflation for 10 years, no deposits or costs, I calculate £1,628.89 nominal and £1,212.05 of starting-year buying power. I checked 1,000 × 1.05¹⁰ by calculator and divided by 1.03¹⁰ for real value. Raising only inflation leaves nominal growth unchanged. I replaced ‘guaranteed savings’ with ‘conditional model output’ because the rate is assumed.”

Keep your complete attempt log and revised card as the paper-route record. No instructor response is required.
